transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-09-04 15:00 PT
- Duration: ~54 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Reyes (Redwood AE), Priya Kaur (Redwood SE), Ethan Marsh (Northbridge VP Eng), Diane Park (Platform Lead), Marco Ruiz (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Northbridge is evaluating Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated for a streaming + batch token workload. Primary concerns: p95 latency targets (~350ms for short chats, 1.2s for longer streams), sustained concurrency of ~1.2k TPS equivalent across 3 regions, and graceful fallback during bursts. They want a 48h hosted benchmark and a short Dedicated trial. Security and audit logs are gating factors.

Topics covered:
- p95 targets and what we measure (inference p95 vs end-to-end)
- streaming vs non-streaming token/sec tradeoffs
- synthetic benchmark plan and artifacts (k6, JMeter, custom harness)
- Dedicated pool sizing and burst capacity
- data residency, SOC2, KMS integration

Questions surfaced:
- How does Redwood account for tokenization differences when measuring token/sec?
- What is cold-start behavior and how is KV cache warmed?
- How do fallbacks to smaller quantized variants affect latency/p95?

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Jordan: Hey everybody, thanks for joining — I'm Jordan with Redwood, and with me is Priya our systems engineer. Um, quick intro — we'll take 30–40 minutes, go over your workload shape and then talk bench, ok?
[00:00:12] Ethan: Yep, thanks Jordan. I'm Ethan, VP Eng at Northbridge. Diane and Marco are on as well, we'll probably jump in with details. We put some numbers in the doc, but happy to walk through.
[00:00:28] Diane: Hi all. Our main prod is a streaming chat assistant + nightly batch embeddings. For the streaming path we target p95 user-perceived latency ~350 milliseconds for short prompts (~40 tokens) and up to 1.2 seconds for long flows when we stream.
[00:00:42] Marco: And on concurrency we typically see bursts up to 1.2k concurrent requests across NA/EU/APAC, steady at ~350 concurrent during day.
[00:00:55] Priya: Cool, couple clarifying Qs — when you say p95, is that strictly model inference or end-to-end with network and front-end?
[00:01:03] Diane: End-to-end as we see it in RUM. We can provide traces but we also want to understand what Redwood measures as model p95 so we can map the gap.
[00:01:18] Jordan: Yeah, great point. Redwood usually reports inference-level p95 (server-side token generation). We also provide routing + network breakdown in the console. For mapping to your RUM numbers we'll run distributed traces in the benchmark.
[00:01:32] Ethan: For benchmarking we want token/sec peak and sustained metrics, and a streaming scenario that reproduces your chunked output — e.g., initial partial tokens then streaming deltas.
[00:01:46] Priya: That's doable. We typically run two passes: a cold-start heavy run to simulate zero warm caches, then a steady-state 2–4 hour run with prefix caching and KV warm. For streaming we emulate chunked sends at 50–100ms intervals.
[00:02:03] Marco: How do you warm KV cache? We have sessions where tokens accumulate and we care about prefix reuse — cold-starts are painful.
[00:02:11] Priya: We pre-seed KV caches by replaying representative prefixes across the worker pool, and we measure the effect on p95. The tool will annotate cache hits vs misses. Note sometimes logs call it "kay-vee cache" in transcripts — sorry on the speech, it's KV.
[00:02:26] Diane: Also curious: tokenization differences across models — our client does BPE, and token counts vary model to model. How do you normalize token/sec?
[00:02:36] Jordan: We report tokens as model-specific tokens, and in the bench we include both token counts and character/sec so you can normalize. We'll also output a tokenization map for the prompt set so you can translate.
[00:02:49] Ethan: Good. On Dedicated — we need predictable throughput. What kind of burst overcommit can we expect to handle without latency cliffs?
[00:02:59] Priya: Dedicated pools allow for burst buffers. Example: a 16-GPU pool with autoscale can sustain steady-state ~X token/sec (we'll provide exact numbers based on model). Burst headroom is controlled by the autoscale and reserved burst credits; for critical apps we recommend a small overprovision or enable burst capacity in the contract.
[00:03:20] Marco: Can you quantify "X"? We need hypothetical numbers to size.
[00:03:26] Priya: Right now I'm high-level in this call — but as an example for a 7B quantized model on A100-equivalent, a single GPU can do ~6k tokens/sec steady and peak upwards if batched. But the exact depends on seq length and attention pattern; we'll run model-specific runs during the trial.
[00:03:47] Ethan: That 6k number, is that per GPU tokens/sec for generation at 1 token per step? Our prompts average 120 tokens output.
[00:03:55] Priya: That baseline is per second for single-token generation steady-state. For longer outputs you multiply by expected tokens/time; we also track tokens per second for both prompt tokens and generated tokens.
[00:04:07] Diane: For streaming, user-perceived p95 is more about first-token latency and then per-chunk latency. Do you instrument both?
[00:04:15] Jordan: Yes, we capture first-byte latency and inter-chunk gaps. In the console you can see the p95 for first token and p95 for streaming chunk intervals.
[00:04:25] Marco: Regarding fallbacks — if a big spike happens and Dedicated hits limits, do you have automatic fallback to Hosted or smaller models?
[00:04:33] Priya: We can implement routing policies: fallback to a quantized variant, or route to Hosted pool if configured in your policy. Fallback adds routing latency but keeps the app online. We track those circuit events in tracing.
[00:04:47] Ethan: Ok makes sense. Security question — we need HSM/KMS integration and audit logs for model access. Any blockers?
[00:04:56] Jordan: Redwood Private supports customer KMS integrations and we surface audit logs for every request. For Hosted we support envelope encryption and we have SOC2; we'll send the security packet after this call.
[00:05:09] Diane: We'll need to run an internal security review before trial — so send the whitepaper and SOC2 link.
[00:05:14] Jordan: Absolutely.
[00:05:19] Priya: Back to bench: can you share the traffic shape — average payload size, percent streaming vs non-streaming, and percent of requests that use function/tool calls?
[00:05:28] Marco: Sure — quick numbers: 65% streaming chat, 30% short sync text gen, 5% embeddings. Median output length ~80 tokens, mean ~120, 99th ~900. Function calls present in ~8% of flows.
[00:05:45] Priya: That's super helpful. We'll craft the synthetic set to match that tail behavior — we definitely want to stress the 99th-case since it drives p95.
[00:05:53] Ethan: For the hosted benchmark window — what's the minimum time you need to give statistically stable p95 numbers?
[00:06:01] Priya: For steady-state I'd say at least 2 hours, but we prefer 4 hours for better confidence on p95 and to capture any autoscale events. For cold-start we do repeated short bursts across nodes.
[00:06:13] Diane: If we do a Dedicated trial, can we reserve capacity only in NA and burst to Hosted in EU/APAC?
[00:06:21] Jordan: Yep, routing policies can be regionalized. You can pin NA to Dedicated and leave EU/APAC to Hosted with a fallback. We'll show cost and latency tradeoffs in the sizing doc.
[00:06:33] Marco: What's the typical rollback behavior if a canary shows quality regressions when you change model weights?
[00:06:39] Priya: We have canary policies with automatic rollback if quality metrics degrade above your threshold. You can define prompt sets and thresholds; the console will flag regressions and either pause rollout or rollback depending on policy.
[00:06:52] Ethan: Do you have pro-tips for token batching to reduce unit cost without breaking streaming latencies?
[00:06:59] Priya: Yes: use micro-batching in the runtime for short time windows (20–30ms) to improve GPU utilization while keeping first-token latency bounded. Also prefix caching reduces repeated compute for common prompts. There's a sweet spot — we'll recommend batch sizes based on your distribution.
[00:07:15] Diane: On metrics — we need per-route cost and token breakdown by prompt vs completion. Is that available?
[00:07:21] Jordan: Yes, per-route token cost, and you can filter by model version and time-range. We'll show an example during the follow-up.
[00:07:30] Marco: We use SSO via SAML and RBAC with fine-grained roles. Is that supported for Dedicated/Private?
[00:07:36] Jordan: Both Dedicated and Private support SAML and AD integrations and RBAC. For Private we can also map to your internal groups.
[00:07:45] Ethan: Ok, next — what's the typical lead time for provisioning a small Dedicated pool?
[00:07:51] Priya: For a trial we can provision a small reserved pool within 2–3 business days if capacity is available; full enterprise setups with network peering and KMS can take 2–4 weeks.
[00:08:02] Diane: For the 48-hour hosted bench — what data do you need from us to configure it?
[00:08:07] Priya: We need representative prompts, tokenization examples, traffic ratios, target p95s, and any blacklisted words/sensitive payload rules. Also the IP allowlist for your test clients.
[00:08:19] Marco: We'll export prompts and a sample trace.
[00:08:23] Jordan: Great. One more thing — during the bench we can collect model-specific kernel stats; sometimes folks see artifacts from specific attention windows that affect long-tail p95. We'll include those diagnostics.
[00:08:37] Ethan: About costs — how should we think about Dedicated vs Hosted for our traffic shape (burst-heavy streaming)?
[00:08:44] Jordan: Short answer: Dedicated reduces unit cost at scale and gives predictable latency, but needs commit or reserved pricing. Hosted is flexible and good for cross-region burst absorb. Our Optimize tool will run a what-if based on your traffic and show cost/latency curves.
[00:08:58] Diane: Can we do a hybrid — Dedicated for NA steady-state and Hosted as overflow?
[00:09:03] Jordan: Yes, that's a common pattern. You get predictable p95 in NA and Hosted absorbs spikes elsewhere or overflow.
[00:09:12] Marco: Any known gotchas with streaming and chunked outputs when using fallback quantized variants?
[00:09:18] Priya: Quantized variants sometimes slightly change tokenization and can increase per-chunk latency marginally. We recommend regression tests with your prompt set — the canary flow will validate that.
[00:09:30] Ethan: Ok excellent. I think we have enough to start a bench. To confirm next steps: Priya will design the synthetic load and Jordan will send pricing and security docs. Northbridge will provide traffic shapes and a prompt dump.
[00:09:42] Jordan: Yup that's the plan. Anything else?
[00:09:46] Diane: Could you include an example of the console view for streaming p95 and first-byte histograms?
[00:09:51] Jordan: We'll attach screenshots in the follow-up email.
[00:09:55] Marco: One last quick note — we have a procurement freeze window mid-September, so would prefer to start bench before Sept 15.
[00:10:03] Jordan: Noted, we'll aim to have the hosted window in the week of Sept 8.
[00:10:08] Ethan: Great. Thanks everyone.

[00:10:20] --- wrap up / off-mic small talk omitted ---
